We evaluate the method on synchrotron tomography of concrete, lens-coupled laboratory microCT of powders, and industrial XCT of additively manufactured metal. Without instrument-specific modeling, we show that SF-Flow achieves substantially higher template agreement and joint fidelity--structure score than previous methods, including contrastive unpaired translation.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: SalivaryHSI-Seg: A New Challenging Benchmark for Ex Vivo Salivary Gland Hyperspectral Tissue Segmentation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Salivary gland tumors are common lesions in oral and maxillofacial practice, and accurate identification of tumor regions and surrounding salivary gland tissues is important for tissue assessment, pathological sampling, and clinical decision support. Hyperspectral imaging (HSI) records continuous spectral responses together with spatial imaging information, providing a promising way to capture fine-grained tissue-discriminative information. Nevertheless, the development of salivary gland HSI tissue segmentation remains limited due to the lack of standardized benchmarks with pixel-level annotations and unified evaluation protocols. To address this issue, we introduce SalivaryHSI-Seg, a hyperspectral tissue segmentation benchmark for ex vivo salivary gland specimens, containing 119 HSI samples from 31 patients with multi-class pixel-level annotations. We establish a patient-level five-fold cross-validation protocol and evaluate different input representations, model architectures, and challenging subsets with small tumor and complex boundary. Based on this benchmark, we further propose HyBSD, a hyperspectral boundary-guided spectral-difference network for full-HSI salivary gland tissue segmentation. HyBSD exploits boundary-guided spectral-difference cues to improve tissue delineation in ambiguous transition regions. Extensive experiments show that full-HSI input provides more discriminative information than sampled spectrums, and that HyBSD achieves 74.97% mDice and 87.76% Tumor Dice, with further advantages on the challenging subsets. Dataset and code will be released.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Pixel as the Common Language: Unified Multimodal Embedding via Visual Rendering
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Multimodal embedding models map heterogeneous inputs into a shared representation space, yet text-only, image-only, and composed inputs are still presented in distinct formats and follow different routes through the model. This fragmentation prevents heterogeneous tasks from jointly optimizing the same end-to-end encoding process, limiting supervision transfer across input configurations. To address this issue, we propose unification before encoding and instantiate this paradigm in RenderEmbed. The framework uses Visual Substrate Rendering to convert heterogeneous inputs into a common visual substrate for encoding with a VLM. From the resulting visual tokens, Progressive Hierarchical Anchor Encoding produces compact retrieval representations by interleaving learnable anchors and fusing their states across layers, retaining broad context and fine-grained cues. Interventional Rendering Learning trains these representations to remain sensitive to content changes and stable across rendering variations through complementary semantic and rendering interventions. Extensive experiments on MMEB and ViDoRe v2, spanning diverse retrieval tasks, show that RenderEmbed outperforms prior state-of-the-art models at the same scale and exhibits strong out-of-domain generalization. Compared with MetaEmbed, RenderEmbed improves MMEB Overall Precision@1 by 1.7 points, with a larger 2.1-point gain on out-of-domain tasks. Transfer and scaling analyses further show that a shared visual pathway enables more effective learning from heterogeneous supervision.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: FolioWeaver: A LayerGraph-Grounded Agent for Layered Image Generation and Editing
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Layered image generation separates images into compositable layers, allowing users to manipulate individual elements independently. However, such asset-level editability does not enable the generation system to interpret successive feedback, perform targeted edits, and preserve unaffected content. We introduce FolioWeaver, a LayerGraph-grounded agent that unifies layered-image generation and iterative editing through a persistent Executable Scene State. FolioWeaver constructs a LayerGraph and generates independent visual assets conditioned on a shared scene reference. An Editing Agent performs feedback-driven modifications and self-repair through scoped actions, selective layer execution, and visual verification, enabling targeted updates while reusing unchanged assets. We also publicly release LayerFolio, a dataset of 100,377 human-reviewed layered scenes spanning six visual domains, together with two evaluation protocols: AtomicQA for measuring requirement satisfaction and CBLP for assessing layer organization. Experiments demonstrate that FolioWeaver achieves superior layer organization and composite fidelity compared with direct layered-generation methods. Analyses validate the contributions of component adaptation, execution-grounded repair, and cross-domain training. FolioWeaver advances layered-image generation toward persistent, controllable, and iterative visual creation. The dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/FolioWeaver/LayerFolio.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: WordEval: Evaluating Word-Native Operation Fidelity in Document Editing
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Microsoft Word is a central environment for office automation, and the faithful execution of its editing operations is an important capability for document agents. Unlike plain-text editing, editing in Word modifies a structured object model, where the requested effect is realized in object properties. Existing benchmarks, however, evaluate office workflows or desktop automation, treating word-processor documents as one task domain among many and verifying outcomes with keyword matching, per-task property checks, or screenshot comparison. We introduce WordEval, an operation-fidelity benchmark that instead centers evaluation on Word editing operations, testing whether each requested edit is realized as intended changes to Word objects and properties. It contains 642 cases across 15 Word feature areas, ranging from text and lists to charts, shape geometry, and SmartArt. 546 atomic cases cover 231 commands, 96 compositional cases combine multiple edits in a single document, and a Word-native oracle checks task-specific object properties and preservation conditions. Cases are constructed from editing-unit specifications, yielding controlled input documents, reference documents, and aligned oracle checks. Each compositional case is linked to corresponding atomic cases, supporting fine-grained diagnosis of editing failures. We evaluate eight agent systems and find that many struggle on the Atomic track, with performance varying across feature areas. Moreover, every system scores lower on Compositional than on Atomic, with gaps that vary substantially by system. Exact atomic-intent links and recorded failure diagnoses provide complementary views of this variation.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Evaluations and Datasets Track). Project page with code and data at https://aka.ms/word-eval

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Regularizing Hard Examples Improves Adversarial Robustness
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Recent studies have validated that pruning hard-to-learn examples from training improves the generalization performance of neural networks (NNs). In this study, we investigate this intriguing phenomenon -- the negative effect of hard examples on generalization -- in adversarial training. Particularly, we theoretically demonstrate that the increase in the difficulty of hard examples in adversarial training is significantly greater than the increase in the difficulty of easy examples. Furthermore, we verify that hard examples are only fitted through memorization of the label in adversarial training. We conduct both theoretical and empirical analyses of this memorization phenomenon, showing that pruning hard examples in adversarial training can enhance the model's robustness. However, the challenge remains in finding the optimal threshold for removing hard examples that degrade robustness performance. Based upon these observations, we propose a new approach, difficulty proportional label smoothing (DPLS), to adaptively mitigate the negative effect of hard examples, thereby improving the adversarial robustness of NNs. Notably, our experimental result indicates that our method can successfully leverage hard examples while circumventing the negative effect.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: 48 pages, 16 figures, 22 tables. Published in the Journal of Machine Learning Research (JMLR)

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: EgoCaptioner: Towards Comprehensive and Fine-Grained Egocentric Video Captioning
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Egocentric video captioning requires fine-grained detail and accurate timing, yet current multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often miss brief actions, confuse their order, or misinterpret the wearer's motion. Existing caption formats also offer limited support for combining detailed narration with precise timing. We present EgoCaptioner, which pairs a video-level overview of the setting, participants, and the wearer's overall activity with timed steps whose narration adapts to varying perceptual demands and marks key moments at specific timestamps. We develop a coarse-to-fine annotation pipeline that establishes event structure before expanding step descriptions, yielding 50,000 training examples from eight egocentric video sources. Complementary rewards assess factual accuracy and coverage, measure step-level temporal alignment, and penalize fragmented or redundant narration, guiding caption refinement through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). To improve the reliability of factual supervision, we supplement caption references with pose-derived motion facts when sensor data are available. Across five egocentric benchmarks, EgoCaptioner achieves leading performance among evaluated open-source models in caption quality, caption-conditioned question answering, and temporal alignment. It also surpasses Gemini 3.1 Pro on PhysCapBench and all evaluated proprietary baselines on Minerva-Ego under the caption-to-QA protocol. Ablations support the complementary roles of factual and temporal rewards and show that coarse-to-fine annotation provides more effective supervision than single-pass annotation.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Mem-X: A Memory-Dependent Cross-Episode Benchmark for Vision-and-Language Navigation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Long-term memory enables embodied agents to reuse past observations across tasks. However, existing cross-episode vision-and-language navigation (VLN) benchmarks often leave it unclear whether successful navigation relies on historical memory or current exploration. We introduce Mem-X, a benchmark designed to evaluate memory-dependent cross-episode VLN. Mem-X organizes episodes into sessions in which subsequent instructions refer to objects or routes encountered in earlier episodes. Its three levels evaluate historical-object recall, in-memory localization and episodic indexing, and off-memory relocalization and historical-route reproduction. For the latter two levels, agents receive episode-local poses but no transformations between episode frames, requiring them to establish spatial correspondence with historical memory. Mem-X comprises 2,071 episodes across 710 sessions in 34 scenes, including 1,204 memory-dependent episodes. We also provide MemBridge, a modular baseline that combines semantic scene memory, cross-episode localization, and coarse-to-fine retrieval to support existing VLN agents. Experiments with state-of-the-art VLN methods demonstrate the benefits of MemBridge while revealing substantial room for improvement on memory-dependent navigation. The benchmark and baseline code are available at https://github.com/NJU-R-L-Group-Embodied-Lab/Mem-X.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: 9 pages, 3 figures. Submitted to IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA 2027)

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Beyond Binary Correctness: A Surrogate for Confidence Learning in Large Language and Vision-Language Models
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Confidence estimation for large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) aims to assess how likely a particular generated response is to be correct. We investigate how learning this assessment can benefit from the model's predictive reliability on the underlying query. Binary correctness supervision, however, assigns identical labels to occasional errors and frequent failures, as well as isolated successes and consistent success. These outcomes can arise from substantially different predictive behavior under stochastic decoding. We propose a confidence-learning framework that supplements realized response correctness with query-level predictive reliability. We estimate reliability through repeated generations under a fixed model and decoding configuration, then combine the empirical success rate with individual correctness to construct a graded confidence surrogate. The surrogate differentiates responses sharing the same correctness label while preserving the average predictive reliability of the sampled response pool. To learn this target, we condition an independent confidence estimator on the query and its full generated response, and optimize backbone LoRA adapters together with a projection and scalar confidence head using mean squared error. Repeated sampling is required only for supervision construction; inference scores an individual response without additional generations. We establish ordering and mean preservation properties of the surrogate and derive a selective-risk bound connecting population surrogate prediction error to the error rate among accepted responses. We evaluate the framework across language and vision-language models, examining confidence calibration and selective prediction.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: FireDesmoke: Fire Smoke Removal via Real Smoke Transfer and Semantic Rectification
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Fire smoke removal must restore dense and medium smoke regions while preserving the clear (smoke-free) content. Existing methods either leave the smoke or alter the visible content, and generative models may hallucinate people or remove flames. Real fire smoke is spatially local: the degradation and its corruption of semantic features are both concentrated in the smoke regions. We propose FireDesmoke, built on this locality: Real Smoke Transfer calibrates smoke fields on real-fire recordings and transfers their spatial layout onto clean images to synthesize training pairs, and Semantic Rectification uses pixel features to rectify the tokens of a frozen foundation encoder where smoke corrupts them. With matched training budgets, replacing the transferred pairs with SmokeBench pairs lowers dense-smoke PSNR by 0.74 dB, and removing Semantic Rectification leaves clear regions 1.31 dB below the input. On what is, to the best of our knowledge, the first paired dataset of real fire smoke for image restoration, with 1,500 test frames from a held-out viewpoint, FireDesmoke improves dense- and medium-smoke PSNR by 3.73 and 2.63 dB while keeping clear regions at the input level (+0.41 dB); no other compared method gains at least 1 dB in dense smoke without lowering clear-region PSNR, and no hallucinated person is found in its outputs. It achieves state-of-the-art overall results on this benchmark and, trained on SmokeBench, the highest PSNR with the second-best SSIM and LPIPS.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Bi-Refine: Semantic Verification-Guided Progressive Refinement for Moment Retrieval
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Moment Retrieval (MR) aims to identify the temporal segment in an untrimmed video that corresponds to a natural language query. Existing approaches commonly refine temporal predictions within the localization pathway, without explicitly verifying candidate-level semantic consistency. Moreover, directly reusing semantic scores as feedback can cause over-correction when the verification signal is unreliable. To address these issues, we propose Bi-Refine, a semantic verification-guided progressive refinement framework that formulates MR as a closed-loop verification-and-refinement process. A Heuristic Localization Branch first generates candidate moments, while a Semantic Verification Branch evaluates their query consistency in a semantically enriched latent space. Query supervision further trains the verifier with the same candidate moment but different queries, encouraging it to distinguish the matched query from semantically similar mismatched queries. The resulting verification features are incorporated into a Progressive Refinement Loop that updates both query representations and multimodal features. To suppress potentially harmful updates, a lightweight reliability estimator gates query updates and reweights candidate contributions in feature feedback. A convergence-based adaptive stopping strategy additionally terminates unnecessary refinement during inference. Experiments on three standard MR benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and state-of-the-art performance of our method.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: What Helps Denoising Can Hurt Memory: Rethinking History in Long Video Generation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Autoregressive video generators produce videos block by block from historical context. They are trained within a bounded horizon, whereas inference can extend far beyond it, causing temporal consistency to gradually decrease. Existing methods focus on eliminating this mismatch, but we instead ask whether the historical context used in training remains suitable for inference. Each block reads historical context in two stages, when denoising generates it and when committing writes it into the KV cache for later blocks. We find that older historical context such as the sink helps denoising but can hurt later blocks when read during committing, even in generators trained to read it there. We also show that as committing reads more preceding blocks, clip-to-clip Subject Consistency rises, plateaus, and then declines. We therefore propose Commit Forcing, a training-free rule that organizes committing into a chain. Each committing pass reads only the preceding block's stored KV, while denoising keeps the base historical context. Commit Forcing improves 60-second VBench Quality and Total on all 6 generators, by up to 1.27 and 1.10 points. Its consistency gains extend to 240-second videos, and it achieves an 82.9% win rate in overall human preference on 120-second LongLive videos.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: 42 pages, 11 figures, 49 tables.Revised text and figures. Clarified experimental protocols and streamlined appendices

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: PsyDrift: Healthy-Reference Latent Diffusion for Anomaly Scoring in Autism Spectrum Disorder
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Individual heterogeneity and acquisition-site variability complicate neuroimaging-based characterization of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). We propose PsyDrift, combining ASD/healthy-control-supervised functional-connectivity representations with healthy-reference latent diffusion. An encoder produces 128-dimensional representations, and a denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) learns exclusively from healthy training latents. Distance from a diffusion-denoised reconstruction provides a continuous deviation score. We evaluate 1,102 subjects from all 20 ABIDE-I sites using five-seed leave-one-site-out cross-validation. The classifier and DDPM achieve mean-site AUROCs of $0.798 \pm 0.003$ and $0.718 \pm 0.013$, respectively; uncertainties denote seed standard deviations. Matched healthy-reference scorers on the same representation achieve 0.68-0.71; the statistical significance of diffusion's modest numerical advantage remains unestablished. Within ASD, scores show weak associations with ADOS Total (Spearman $ρ= 0.108$, $p = 0.038$) and full-scale IQ ($ρ= -0.138$, $p = 0.002$), without adjustment for age, sex, site, or head motion. Frozen evaluation without retraining or hyperparameter adaptation yields pooled AUROCs of 0.69 on ABIDE-II and 0.61 on ADHD-200, providing preliminary evidence of cross-cohort and cross-disorder transfer. These results demonstrate healthy-reference deviation scoring within an ASD-supervised representation; incremental predictive and clinical value remains unestablished.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Extended version of a paper accepted at the CVPath-Vision4Neuro Workshop at WACV 2027. Includes expanded related-work and future-work discussion

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: SWAM: State-aware World Action Model for Multi-Agent 3D Environments
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Interactive world models generate virtual environments autoregressively from player actions and visual history. However, visual history alone cannot reliably capture the evolving states of independently acting non-player characters (NPCs) in real games, particularly when they are outside the camera view. Recent multi-agent world models address this challenge through joint multi-view generation or persistent shared state, but often rely on external observations, like maps or scene geometry, or predefined state transitions. We present SWAM, a State-aware World Action Model that separates agent-state evolution from autoregressive visual generation in interactive 3D environments. A lightweight state model propagates character dynamics from actions without consuming generated frames, combining motion priors with learned scene-dependent corrections. The predicted states then guide an autoregressive diffusion transformer alongside visual history through a novel conditioning scheme. Rather than requiring an explicit scene geometry map or visibility tests, the conditioning indicates where characters may appear, allowing the diffusion model to learn their appearance and occlusion. This design enables NPCs to evolve independently of visual generation while maintaining consistent observations across visibility changes, interactions, and respawns. Evaluations in a custom Godot-based first-person shooter game demonstrate improvements in visual fidelity, NPC consistency, and long-horizon stability over existing approaches.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Teaching How to Reason, Beyond What to Answer: Evidence-Faithful On-Policy Distillation for streaming video understanding
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Moment Retrieval (MR) aims to localize the temporal segment in a video that corresponds to a given textual description. However, a textual query often provides only a sparse semantic description of the target event, whereas the video contains rich and fine-grained visual variations. This mismatch creates an inherent gap between textual semantics and visual content, making a single textual input insufficient for precise cross-modal alignment. As a result, when multiple temporally adjacent or semantically similar segments exist, the model may struggle to distinguish the target moment from confusing candidates. To address this challenge, we propose a Multi-Perspective Auxiliary Representation (MPAR) framework, which aims to bridge this alignment gap by enriching a single textual input with complementary visual cues from multiple perspectives. Specifically, MPAR consists of three key components: (1) Auxiliary Representation Initialization (ARI) constructs multiple learnable representation slots from the original query, preserving the query intent while preparing flexible carriers for subsequent visual cue injection; (2) Visual-Induced Semantic Structuring (VISS) injects target-specific visual attributes into each representation while preserving semantic coherence with the original query; and (3) Multi-Perspective Semantic Aligner (MPSA) aligns each auxiliary representation with corresponding video regions to enhance discriminative localization. By constructing multi-perspective auxiliary representations and guiding the model to attend to relevant visual regions across these representations, our model achieves more accurate moment localization. Extensive experiments on MR benchmarks demonstrate that our MPAR outperforms state-of-the-art methods, validating the effectiveness of MPAR.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Cross-modal RAG: Sub-dimensional Text-to-Image Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Text-to-image generation increasingly demands access to domain-specific, fine-grained, and rapidly evolving knowledge that pretrained models cannot fully capture, necessitating the integration of retrieval methods. Existing Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) methods attempt to address this by retrieving globally relevant images, but they fail when no single image contains all desired elements from a complex user query. We propose Cross-modal RAG, a novel framework that decomposes both queries and images into sub-dimensional components, enabling subquery-aware retrieval and generation. Our method introduces a hybrid retrieval strategy, combining a sub-dimensional sparse retriever with a dense retriever, to identify a Pareto-optimal set of images, each contributing complementary aspects of the query. During generation, a multimodal large language model is guided to selectively condition on relevant visual features aligned to specific subqueries for subquery-aware image synthesis. Extensive experiments on MS-COCO, Flickr30K, WikiArt, CUB, and ImageNet-LT demonstrate that Cross-modal RAG significantly outperforms existing baselines in the retrieval and further contributes to generation quality, while maintaining high efficiency.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: QSRadar: Query-Conditioned Sparse Radar-Camera Fusion for Efficient 3D Object Detection
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Reliable 3D object detection for autonomous trucks requires both the semantic detail provided by cameras and the geometric and motion cues measured by 4D radar. Existing radar-camera detectors commonly construct global radar bird's-eye-view (BEV) representations, whose computational and memory costs grow with the perception range. Sparse query-based detectors offer greater efficiency, but global feature construction can obscure point-level radar geometry and motion information. We present QSRadar, a query-conditioned sparse radar fusion framework for efficient long-range 3D detection. Built on a Sparse4Dv3-style visual-temporal detector, QSRadar retrieves a compact set of raw radar points around each evolving object hypothesis. The selected points are represented in an anchor-aligned coordinate frame, augmented with motion residuals, radar cross section, and sweep timing, and aggregated by a query-conditioned set encoder. Radar neighborhoods are retrieved again after each anchor refinement, coupling evidence selection with object estimation. Under the official MAN TruckScenes validation protocol, QSRadar achieves 38.09 mAP and 52.20 NDS, compared with 37.08 mAP and 50.78 NDS for our reproduced Sparse4D-Radar global Radar-BEV baseline. In matched tests on an RTX 4090 D, QSRadar reduces latency by 45%, peak memory usage by 49%, and GFLOPs by 43%.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Radar-camera fusion, 3D object detection, autonomous driving

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: PACT: Plan-Action Consistency Training by Preserving Correct Plans and Repairing Actions in GUI Agents
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: GUI agents can formulate a correct immediate plan in their reasoning yet emit an action that fails to execute it, creating an execution gap. This recurring mismatch undermines reliable task completion, as a single execution error can derail a multi-step workflow. In outcome-supervised reinforcement learning, broadcasting a negative response-level advantage across all generated tokens risks penalizing valid planning together with erroneous execution. To address this credit-assignment conflict, we introduce PACT (Plan-Action Consistency Training), a training framework that combines reference-aligned plan protection and plan-aligned action repair without altering the original scalar action reward. Using annotated reference actions to identify execution gaps, PACT protects the verified plan by masking negative policy-gradient contributions across its token span. Keeping the generated reasoning unchanged as context, it then favors the reference action over the emitted erroneous action through a preference surrogate with stop-gradient pair weights. Compared with the outcome-only baseline, PACT raises AndroidWorld task success from 60.34% to 68.97% (+8.63 pp), while improving rule-based plan-action consistency on AndroidControl High from 83.71% to 89.74% (+6.03 pp). Adapting PACT to desktop agents also improves task success from 40.92% to 44.17% (+3.25 pp) on the full 369-task OSWorld benchmark. Together, these results establish PACT as an effective credit-assignment framework for bridging execution gaps and improving task completion across mobile and desktop GUI environments.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: 21 pages, 11 figures, including supplementary material. This version clarifies implementation details and evaluation protocols in the supplementary material

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: MOVER: Planning Beyond Motion
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Residual world models forecast a driving scene through its temporal change, so feature components that stay constant over time vanish from the residual pathway. We ask whether evidence with weak temporal change, such as a waiting pedestrian or a stopped vehicle, can be used more effectively for planning, and introduce MOVER, a complementary event-routing mechanism. A training-time teacher measures how each spatially grounded event query responds when a past frame is removed from shared history and contrasts that sensitivity with the event's pooled temporal residual, prioritizing events that depend on history but receive weak residual evidence. A student predicts the resulting priorities from unperturbed history, so the teacher adds no inference cost. Under fixed total routing mass, one distribution scales a low-rank future bird's-eye-view update and biases trajectory-conditioned event reading. On nuScenes, MOVER reduces ResWorld's UniAD-style average L2 from 0.65 to 0.55 m and its collision rate from 0.23% to 0.12% without direct planner ego status (0.50 m and 0.09% with it), adding 4.1 ms per frame. Matched controls show that the complementary teacher outperforms either signal alone and that the allocation acts mainly during training. Adapted to BridgeDrive-LEAD, MOVER reaches a 96.52 +/- 0.65 driving score over three seeds on the 220-route Bench2Drive closed-loop benchmark, exceeding matched controls in each paired seed by a margin within seed variation.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: ReplaySAM: Zero-Shot 3D Particle-Pack Segmentation with SAM 2
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: X-ray computed tomography (XCT) provides non-destructive three-dimensional (3D) images of particle packs, making their internal structure accessible for quantitative analysis. Extracting particle-level measurements from these volumes first requires identifying and separating individual particles, a task that remains challenging in dense, irregular packs. Existing workflows often require manual correction or task-specific training, while promptable models need a strategy for automatically locating individual particles and recovering their instance masks. We present ReplaySAM, which adapts the pretrained Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2) to three-dimensional particle-pack segmentation without additional training. It generates point prompts from foreground geometry and fuses SAM2 predictions across orthogonal slice sequences to recover particle instances. On XCT volumes of real quartz and iron-ore particle packs, ReplaySAM achieves higher mean instance Dice scores than expert-assisted watershed and nnInteractive under the evaluated protocols. ReplaySAM thus provides a training-free framework for 3D particle-pack instance segmentation, with geometry-based prompting that eliminates manual prompt placement.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: 3AGameFactory-Motion: Agentic Rigging and Reliable Complex Motion Generation for Diverse 3D Assets
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Animating arbitrary 3D assets from instructions requires both structural inference and motion control, yet existing motion benchmarks mostly cover conventional human or animal skeletons with simple instructions. We introduce DivDynBench, which evaluates rigging and motion generation across six morphology categories, with instructions requiring multi-phase part coordination and explicit timing, angle, repetition, and trajectory constraints. With large language models, we systematically compare three common paradigms: specialized motion generation, video generation followed by motion recovery, and direct agent-driven generation. We analyze their control capabilities, cross-morphology adaptability, and generation costs. Guided by this comparison, we propose an Agentic Motion Framework in which an agent writes compact parametric skeleton and motion programs, and a deterministic executor performs rigging, kinematic solving, and geometric correction. Compact parameter control reduces generation overhead and improves rigging reliability and motion-control accuracy, providing practical guidance for deploying complex 3D motion generation.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: FlexGaze: Weakly Supervised Gaze Estimation at Scale
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Most gaze estimation models are trained on data collected using specialized equipment. The limited diversity of subjects, scenes, and head poses in these datasets hinders generalization to new conditions. We present FlexGaze, a family of 3D gaze estimators pretrained with weak supervision from gaze labels (pseudo-labels) automatically generated from in-the-wild images. We use off-the-shelf models to predict 2D gaze targets and scene depth, then combine these predictions to generate 3D gaze labels for approximately 3.24 million head instances. At inference, FlexGaze predicts gaze from a head crop alone and can handle profile and rear views without requiring face detection or head pose estimation. We use data augmentation during training to improve robustness to variations in crop position and scale. Pretrained using only these generated gaze labels, FlexGaze generalizes to unseen benchmarks. After supervised fine-tuning on public gaze datasets, we evaluate FlexGaze on eight benchmarks under a unified evaluation protocol. Our models match or outperform publicly available gaze estimators with several times as many parameters on most benchmarks. We release our dataset of generated gaze labels, all trained models, and code via https://github.com/ihp-lab/FlexGaze.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: 23 pages, including 12 pages of supplementary material

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: MORSE: Optimizing Streaming Memory Design via Open-World Auto-Research
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: A streaming video system must decide in a single pass what evidence to retain under bounded frame storage, before it knows which details a future question will require. Recent recursive self-improvement methods automate the design of the harness that stores and retrieves this evidence. They revise the harness in response to failures, but the editor must still devise each repair from its prior knowledge and a predefined set of tools. A failure that recurs across videos, however, may point to a problem that prior work has already addressed. We introduce MORSE (Memory Optimization with Recursive Self-Evolvement), an open-world auto-research framework that uses recurring failures to guide an online search for solutions. Its editor groups failures in training traces by cause, then searches papers, model cards, and code for methods it can adapt or pretrained perception models it can use. When the editor introduces a new perceptual capability, it can also revise how the harness stores and retrieves the resulting evidence for a frozen video-language model. On held-out validation streams, MORSE first selects revisions that improve answer quality, then seeks faster revisions that preserve those gains within a specified tolerance. Across three streaming video benchmarks, MORSE consistently achieves the highest answer accuracy within each frozen-backbone comparison. On OVO-Bench, our Qwen3-VL-8B harness answers queries in 0.30 seconds on average while achieving 75.1% accuracy, 3.1 percentage points ahead of the next-best evaluated harness using the same frozen backbone.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Antiphony: A Dual-Process Agent for Deepfake Video Detection with Real-Video Calibration
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Reliable video deepfake detection requires generalization to unseen generators while limiting false alarms on authentic footage. Although existing detectors capture diverse visual cues, they may produce overconfident errors under generator shift, limiting the reliability of confidence-based fusion. Threshold calibration is further complicated by shifts in authentic capture domains and the lack of future-generator examples. To address these challenges, we present Antiphony, a framework that combines calibrated fusion of four visual experts with selective investigation. Authentic videos serve as a shared reference for score fusion and threshold calibration, enabling threshold updates without target deepfakes. For this expert-fusion stage, we establish finite-sample false-alarm control when the scoring procedure is fixed independently of calibration and authentic samples are exchangeable. To refine decisions near the calibrated threshold, a tool-using multimodal investigator examines these videos and contributes an additional fusion score. We train the investigator on generator-held-out predictions and counterfactual expert outputs, to improve robustness to unreliable expert evidence. Across six benchmark protocols, Antiphony achieves a mean benchmark score of 88.3%, exceeding the strongest evaluated MLLM and conventional detector baselines by 14.7 and 11.5 points, respectively. It also outperforms ARGUS by 20.2 points on average and by 3.6 balanced-accuracy points on FaceVid's 20 unseen generators.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: One Size Doesn't Fit All: Input Adaptive Class Activation Mapping for Improved Visual Explanations
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Despite their widespread use in tasks such as image classification, object detection and semantic segmentation, the limited interpretability of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Vision Transformers (ViTs) can undermine trust and hinder adoption in safety-critical applications. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods seek to address this by providing human-understandable explanations for model predictions. Class Activation Maps (CAM) constitute one such widely used XAI technique for visualizing discriminative regions. However, existing CAM methods may exhibit limitations in channel weighting, localization, and adaptability across network architectures potentially resulting in noisy or imprecise explanations. To address these issues, we propose ADAPT-CAM, a gradient-based, parameter-adaptive CAM framework. The method combines first-order gradient energy with activation-weighted second-order curvature to derive channel contributions. It further incorporates adaptive local contrast normalization and knee-guided soft channel selection to refine the resulting explanations. Importantly, key parameters are estimated independently for each input, allowing the framework to adapt to variations in feature representations across network architectures. We validate ADAPT-CAM on ImageNet and Oxford 102 Flowers across CNN and ViT architectures. Quantitative results demonstrate competitive or superior performance against established CAM methods across multiple evaluation metrics. In parallel, qualitative comparisons illustrate its ability to highlight discriminative image regions. Further parameter analysis and ablation experiments examine the behaviour and contributions of the individual adaptive components. These findings demonstrate the applicability of ADAPT-CAM across different architectures and datasets.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Zing-1.0: A Playable World System Built on Controllable Rendering
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: We present Zing-1.0, a Playable World System built on Controllable Rendering. An executable engine resolves player actions under the world's rules and produces proxy video from the updated state. A streaming video model synthesizes the player's view from this proxy, and the runtime delivers it to inform subsequent actions. (1) Principle and system. We formulate Controllable Rendering and define the interfaces among world construction, world execution, observation synthesis, and the interaction runtime. To our knowledge, this is the first implementation-independent specification of a Playable World System. (2) AI-native engine. WorldKit provides structured authoring tools and reusable character, camera, and control components for coding agents to construct executable proxy worlds. It supports extensible interactions and precise geometric motion control while separating executable behavior from final visual appearance. (3) Streaming renderer. We adapt MiniMax-H3 for block-causal autoregressive generation and incremental decoding. Proxy video constrains structure and motion, while text and separate scene and subject references specify appearance. We train the generator on diverse tasks and distill it to generate each block in a few denoising steps. The renderer leads the compared streaming editors on OpenVE (3.90) and LongV2VBench (3.44). On StreamEval, Zing-1.0 scores 57.86 on instruction editing and 54.06 on reference editing, exceeding the published baselines on both tracks. (4) Interaction infrastructure. We build an Interaction Runtime that routes player actions to WorldKit while supporting in-play prompt and reference updates. Cross-block joint execution and sparse attention with compressed K/V reduce inference overhead. With the DiT on a single H200 and encoding and decoding on one H100 each, the serving system achieves a steady-state throughput of 23.82 FPS at $832\times480$.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: 34 pages, 17 figures. Authors listed in reverse alphabetical order by surname. v2 corrects the project link to https://zing.loopit.me/

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Embodied-Harness: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Robotic Manipulation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Vision-language model (VLM)-based agents offer a promising approach to robotic manipulation, yet remain limited by inadequate memory organization, uncertain failure attribution, and limited reuse of execution experience. We propose Embodied-Harness, a dual-agent framework that improves manipulation by refining the execution harness without updating model parameters. The Actor interacts with the environment through a robot-control interface, while the Reflector converts execution evidence into reusable operational guidance. Hierarchical Memory Architecture maintains short-term execution context and long-term experiential knowledge to support execution and reflection. Evidence-based Experience Reflection grounds failure diagnosis in observed interactions, while Recursive Harness Self-Improvement refines operational guidance across successive attempts. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboSPA, and RMBench demonstrate the effectiveness of Embodied-Harness in generalization under environmental variations, spatial reasoning, long-horizon planning, and memory-dependent manipulation. Our method achieves success rates of 82.4%, 76.7%, and 94.4% on the three benchmarks, respectively. Real-world evaluation further yields an average success rate of 96.7% across three manipulation tasks. These results highlight the potential of Embodied-Harness to improve robotic manipulation through experience-driven harness self-improvement.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: FASCIA: Seeing Beneath the Surface with Queryable, Personalized Anatomy in Any Pose
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: We present FASCIA (*Functional Anatomical Structures and Composition via Implicit Atlas*), a Momentum Human Rig (MHR)-anchored framework that predicts and poses a person's internal anatomy from their external body shape and skeletal proportions. FASCIA maps a single 290-structure population template onto each individual through a smooth, invertible warp. As people with the same shape can differ internally, a body-dependent Gaussian prior predicts both average warp coordinates and their inter-subject variability. The warp deforms a learned base template into bones, muscles, organs, and fat depots. Extending MHR skinning into the interior enables direct supervision of this model across four automatically labeled CT cohorts and one whole-body MRI cohort. On 82 held-out CT scans, FASCIA reaches a mean volumetric Dice (volume agreement) of 0.48 on named bones and 0.63 on muscles, keeps the majority of bones and muscles in one piece, and yields calibrated voxel probabilities. On 33 held-out whole-body MRI subjects, FASCIA's pointwise field improves tissue overlap over HIT across all compartments, predicts between-person differences in whole-body adipose percentage ($R^2 = 0.88$ vs. $0.38$ in women and $0.54$ vs. $-0.01$ in men), and recovers segment centers of mass within 1.1 mm. Because it needs only an MHR fit, FASCIA can be driven from images, video, or any system that outputs MHR. This opens the door to fitting individualized calibrated musculoskeletal digital twins to video motion data.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: CARE-3D: Reinforcement Learning for Evidence Grounded Agentic Reasoning in Situated 3D Scenes
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Situated 3D reasoning requires embodied agents to interpret objects, scene geometry, and viewpoint dependent spatial relations. Existing methods learn grounded interactions from supervised traces, but largely imitate prescribed evidence acquisition patterns rather than optimizing the support that the returned evidence provides for the correct answer. Moreover, outcome rewards provide limited credit for intermediate tool choices and may leave infrequent tools underexplored. An effective agent should instead adaptively decide what to ground, which tool to invoke, and how to assess the utility of returned evidence. To this end, this paper presents CARE-3D, a reinforcement post-training framework for adaptive grounded reasoning. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on grounding instructions first establishes valid interactions, after which Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) optimizes the agent while keeping the 3D grounding module frozen. CARE-3D combines Counterfactual Attribution of Returned Evidence for evidence sensitive credit assignment, and Group Coverage Sampling to preserve tool coverage. Experiments on MSQA and Beacon3D show consistent gains over SFT and GRPO using only answer and format rewards, especially in spatial reasoning and grounding answer coherence. Our code is available at \href{https://github.com/xiaoqian-UQ/CARE-3D}{CARE-3D}.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: When Should We Trust Medical Image Models? Evaluating Confidence Reliability under Cross-Dataset Shift
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary:
Deep learning models for chest X-ray analysis often achieve strong performance on benchmark datasets, but their reliability under cross-dataset deployment remains unclear. In clinical practice, models trained in one hospital system may be applied to data from another, where distributional and labeling differences can affect both prediction accuracy and model confidence.
  We conduct a controlled empirical study of model confidence under cross-dataset transfer. We train ResNet-50 and DenseNet-121 on CheXpert and evaluate them on MIMIC-CXR across five experimental settings, focusing on Pneumothorax and Pleural Effusion. We measure predictive performance using AUC and confidence reliability using Expected Calibration Error (ECE), Brier score, and average confidence on incorrect predictions, all reported with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. We further evaluate post-hoc temperature scaling fit on the source validation set and use Grad-CAM to examine the mechanism behind cross-domain performance differences.
  Cross-domain AUC drops 7-13 percentage points, and the best in-domain model is not the best cross-domain model. Source-domain temperature scaling produces marginal ECE changes but systematically increases confidence on incorrect predictions across all four model-pathology combinations. Grad-CAM reveals that DenseNet relies on a concentrated spatial prior that fails to transfer, while ResNet's more distributed attention generalizes better. These findings argue for cross-site validation and safety-specific calibration metrics in medical AI evaluation.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: 7 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Course research project, CS585 Image and Video Computing, Boston University, Spring 2026

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Coarse3D: Controllable and Faithful Sparse Structure Generation for Image-to-3D
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Coarse-to-fine 3D-native generation relies heavily on the first-stage sparse structure, which determines the global orientation and overall geometry for subsequent refinement. However, existing coarse generators suffer from two key limitations: their orientation is difficult to control due to ambiguous semantic canonicalization, and their structures are often inconsistent with input images due to weak 2D-3D grounding. We propose Coarse3D, a sparse-structure generation model that produces orientation-controllable and structurally faithful voxel geometry from arbitrary unposed images. Coarse3D introduces three designs: a first-frame anchored canonical space that aligns generation with the first input view while preserving object-centric normalization; a dual-tower DiT that couples generation with auxiliary feed-forward reconstruction to learn spatially grounded features; and spatial-prior guided attention that regularizes cross-attention with pixel-to-voxel correspondence. Coarse3D can directly replace the coarse stage of existing pipelines. Experiments show that it substantially improves sparse structure quality and consistently enhances final 3D generation, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: We request a withdrawal notice due to an internal data disclosure review issue. A revised version will be submitted after approvals are obtained. We apologize for any inconvenience

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Let LiDAR Decide Where to Look: Geometry-Measured Token Selection for Efficient Sparse Latent World Models
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Vision-centric autonomous driving models encode thousands of image tokens per frame, yet most depict sky, buildings, or empty road---content irrelevant to planning. Worse, these tokens dilute the planner's attention: we show that randomly discarding 75% of tokens already outperforms the dense model, because the planner can concentrate on the remaining driving-critical content. Building on this finding, we present Geometry-Aware Token Selection (GATS), which uses LiDAR and radar point projections to select a small fraction of image tokens before the vision backbone runs. Because the selector operates on measured 3D geometry rather than visual features, the backbone encodes only the selected patches, cutting end-to-end FLOPs by up to $18\times$. Each kept token receives a 3D anchor from its LiDAR point and is fed to a self-supervised latent world model that predicts future features and 3D displacements without box annotations. At 25% budget, GATS achieves a 3-sec L2 displacement error of 0.520 m on nuScenes and an EPDMS of 88.9 on NAVSIM---surpassing the dense baseline (0.573 m / 85.9) at $6.6\times$ fewer total FLOPs. At an extreme 10% budget (24 GFLOPs, $18\times$ reduction), it still beats the dense baseline on both nuScenes (0.537 m vs. 0.573 m L2) and NAVSIM (87.9 vs. 85.9 EPDMS). On 739 intent-critical scenarios, GATS covers 95.8% of hazardous vehicles and achieves a 0.09% collision rate---73.5% lower than the dense model (0.34%).

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Seen but Unsaid: Locating and Repairing Cross-Image Comparison in Vision-Language Models
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) often fail to match a point or an object across two images, even when the match can be decoded from their hidden states. We trace where this information is lost in Qwen3-VL-2B/4B/8B/32B, InternVL3.5-8B, and Gemma-3-12B on synthetic shape matching, HPatches point correspondence, and SPair-71k semantic correspondence, comparing input-matched probes with calibrated outputs. The models fail at two distinct points. Exact copies are compared and the result reaches the answer position, but the output does not use it, whether or not the shapes have names. Semantic correspondences are present in the visual tokens but are only weakly compared and never reach the answer position. The comparison runs through 16 to 32 attention heads that let tokens of the second image attend to the first. Redistributing their attention at fixed mass removes up to 32 points of accuracy, against at most 7 for random or attention-matched heads, and their attention is gated by salience and weighted by content. Training only these heads (0.02% of the parameters) recovers 25 to 28 points on SPair-71k and transfers to HPatches and BLINK. Unconstrained LoRA adapters, which reach higher accuracy, converge on the same heads: inserting only these heads' attention into the base model recovers 21-51% of an adapter's gain, mostly through changed inputs to the heads. Across all 14 trained arms, the selectivity of this small head set tracks the accuracy they reach, and it is read directly from attention, without probes or retraining. The gain in selectivity is not a by-product of more attention to the first image: it comes mostly from the wrong options no longer being drawn to the marked reference.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: 21 pages, 5 figures, 20 tables. v2: added attention-map figure (Fig. 2), repaired-model maps, scale-free selectivity measures, and a table of pre-specified criteria; revised notation and text; corrected references

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: KGLP-Net: Kalman-Reliable Global--Local Learning With Group Fisher Pruning for Hyperspectral Image Classification
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Accurate hyperspectral image (HSI) classification requires both the effective integration of broad spatial context and fine-grained spectral--spatial information surrounding target pixels. However, the reliability of these complementary representations may vary considerably across heterogeneous scenes, and uncertainty estimates obtained during feature fusion are rarely exploited to guide subsequent model compression. To address these challenges, we propose Kalman-Reliable Global--Local Learning with Group Fisher Pruning (KGLP-Net), a unified framework that couples uncertainty-aware feature fusion with reliability-guided structured pruning. Specifically, an asymmetric dual-view architecture employs a Global Mamba Encoder to capture long-range spatial dependencies and a Local CNN Encoder to extract fine-grained spectral--spatial features from target neighborhoods. To adaptively integrate these complementary representations, Kalman-Reliable Fusion (KRF) estimates their relative uncertainties in feature space and performs a Kalman-inspired posterior update, treating global features as a contextual prior and local features as an observation. Building upon the resulting posterior uncertainty, Kalman-Reliable Group Fisher Pruning (KRGF) quantifies group-level reliability through normalized posterior precision and integrates it with Group Fisher importance to identify and prune Kalman-coupled channel groups, enabling structurally consistent model compression. Experiments on four public HSI datasets demonstrate that the resulting Compact48 model, with a hidden width of 48, achieves the highest overall accuracy among ten representative competing classifiers. Compared with the unpruned Dense64 model, Compact48 reduces the number of parameters, FLOPs, and inference time by 38.5%, 34.8% and 37.6% on average, respectively, while incurring only a 0.03-percentage-point decrease in mean overall accuracy.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: HierSum: A Global and Local Attention Mechanism for Video Summarization
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Video summarization creates an abridged version (i.e., a summary) that provides a quick overview of the video while retaining pertinent information. In this work, we focus on summarizing instructional videos and propose a method for breaking down a video into meaningful segments, each corresponding to essential steps in the video. We propose **HierSum**, a hierarchical approach that integrates fine-grained local cues from subtitles with global contextual information provided by video-level instructions. Our approach utilizes the "most replayed" statistic as a supervisory signal to identify critical segments, thereby improving the effectiveness of the summary. We evaluate on benchmark datasets such as TVSum, BLiSS, Mr.HiSum, and the WikiHow test set, and show that HierSum consistently outperforms existing methods in key metrics such as F1-score and rank correlation. We also curate a new multi-modal dataset using WikiHow and EHow videos, and associated articles containing step-by-step instructions. Through extensive ablation studies, we demonstrate that training on this dataset significantly enhances summarization on the target datasets. The code and dataset will be available at https://github.com/ApoorvaBeedu/HierSum.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Accepted at the AI4RWC Workshop, CVPR 2026. Code and dataset: https://github.com/ApoorvaBeedu/HierSum

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Knowledge-Guided Floodwater Level Reasoning for Cloud-Edge Collaborative Monitoring
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Frequent urban floodwater poses a serious threat to the safety and efficiency of intelligent transportation systems. Existing vision-based methods for floodwater level detection face two main limitations. First, the lack of explicit reasoning leads to poor detection performance and little interpretability. Second, these methods struggle to generalize to the complex and varied real-world road scenes seen from different viewpoints. To address this, we reformulate the task as an explicit visual reasoning problem and propose HydroReasoner, a floodwater level reasoning framework designed for cloud-edge collaboration. HydroReasoner builds on Qwen2.5-VL and is trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization. To address the scarcity of reasoning process annotations, we build a floodwater domain knowledge graph HydroKG and design a novel KG path reward. Through deterministic graph traversal over HydroKG, this reward supervises the model's reasoning process at a fine granularity, which improves both reasoning and generalization. For edge deployment, we apply 4-bit quantization to the model, cutting GPU memory usage by 57% and inference latency by 43% while out-of-domain accuracy drops by only 0.2 percentage points. We also propose a confidence-based cloud-edge routing mechanism, which improves system safety and eases the computational load on the cloud. In addition, we build HydroLevel, a floodwater benchmark dataset of 3,000 images, for training and evaluating the model. Experimental results show that HydroReasoner achieves detection accuracy 4.0 and 13.6 percentage points higher than conventional vision baselines in the in-domain and out-of-domain evaluations respectively, with performance dropping by only 4.4 percentage points out of domain.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: This paper has been withdrawn by the authors due to administrative and institutional review requirements

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: StereoAdapter-2: Globally Structure-Consistent Underwater Stereo Depth Estimation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Stereo depth estimation is fundamental to underwater robotic perception, yet suffers from severe domain shifts caused by wavelength-dependent light attenuation, scattering, and refraction. Recent approaches leverage monocular foundation models with GRU-based iterative refinement for underwater adaptation; however, the sequential gating and local convolutional kernels in GRUs necessitate multiple iterations for long-range disparity propagation, limiting performance in large-disparity and textureless underwater regions. In this paper, we propose StereoAdapter-2, which replaces the conventional ConvGRU updater with a novel ConvSS2D operator based on selective state space models. The proposed operator employs a four-directional scanning strategy that naturally aligns with epipolar geometry while capturing vertical structural consistency, enabling efficient long-range spatial propagation within a single update step at linear computational complexity. Furthermore, we construct UW-StereoDepth-80K, a large-scale synthetic underwater stereo dataset featuring diverse baselines, attenuation coefficients, and scattering parameters through a two-stage generative pipeline combining semantic-aware style transfer and geometry-consistent novel view synthesis. Combined with dynamic LoRA adaptation inherited from StereoAdapter, our framework achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot performance on underwater benchmarks with 17% improvement on TartanAir-UW and 7.2% improvment on SQUID, with real-world validation on the BlueROV2 platform demonstrates the robustness of our approach. Code: https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/StereoAdapter-2. Website: https://aigeeksgroup.github.io/StereoAdapter-2.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Benchmarking VLM Medical Hallucination across 5 Modalities
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Hallucinations in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) within the medical domain remain a difficult and not well-understood problem, and it is still unclear where these models break down. Although several benchmarks targeting medical hallucination have been introduced, they often lack broad coverage across different medical imaging modalities. We introduce Multi-Med, a medical hallucination benchmark containing 1,000 image-question pairs spanning five distinct modalities. Using this benchmark, we perform an in-depth experimental study of 10 widely used VLMs across five modalities and four question categories. Our findings indicate that model performance differs substantially depending on the imaging modality and question type, and that the differences among the best-performing models are not statistically significant.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: SCAR: Bridging Coarse Retrieval and Fine Localization through Candidate Reranking
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Natural-language point-cloud localization typically retrieves candidate map cells and then predicts a position inside each candidate, yet the final output is still determined by retrieval order. A retrieval score measures region-description relevance, not whether the coordinates a region yields are accurate: a relevant region may produce a displaced prediction, and a lower-ranked region may contain a successful one. We study the final selection problem after the candidate pool and Fine predictions are fixed---how to choose the coordinate most likely to localize successfully, and under which conditions the gain holds. We propose SCAR (Spatial Consistency-Aware Reranking). SCAR treats each cell--Fine-coordinate pair as a localization hypothesis, interprets directional relations as functions of position, and reads spatial support at the backbone's actual Fine point (Fine-conditioned Evidence Readout). It organizes this readout with center support, semantic presence, retrieval score, and geometric offsets into a 23-D representation, trains a shared scorer with localization-success labels, and at inference reranks existing hypotheses and returns their original coordinates. Experiments cover four public backbones and a corrected Des4Pos reimplementation across five domains. Excluding one protocol-reference configuration, exploratory TEST point estimates on the remaining 24 configurations show Top-1@5\,m above Original on 23 and Cell R@1 above Original on all 24. On development-set VAL, the Fine readout improves Top-1@5\,m by 5.77 percentage points (pp) over a center surrogate on corrected Des4Pos*KITTI, and the complete scoring scheme improves it by 13.98\,pp over FSR on MambaPlace$\times$nuScenesFull; the latter measures the complete scheme, not learned ranking alone.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: SleuthVLM: Do We Really Need Audio-in-Video for Omni Video Understanding?
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Omni models answer questions about videos by jointly processing sampled frames and audio in one turn, while VLMs have become strong agents that can search a video over many turns. We ask how far a model can go without hearing the audio, and present \method, a simple multi-turn harness built on such a VLM that never hears the audio directly: speech is transcribed into text, and the VLM sleuths the video without a predefined workflow. On four omni benchmarks with videos up to 90 minutes, \method achieves the best average accuracy: \textbf{75.0\%}, 2.6 points above Gemini 3.8 Flash, and it tops the Video-MME-v2 leaderboard with \textbf{77.8\%}; with Qwen3.8-27B, it is comparable to open-source omni models on short videos and better on long ones. We draw three insights: searching outperforms passive observation; agentic ability matters as much as direct audio access; and small agentic models are highly competitive. So we provide a simple but effective starting point for omni video understanding.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: SegSTRONG-C: Segmenting Surgical Tools Robustly On Non-adversarial Generated Corruptions -- An EndoVis'24 Challenge
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Surgical data science has seen rapid advancement with the excellent performance of end-to-end deep neural networks (DNNs). Despite their successes, DNNs have been proven susceptible to minor ``corruptions,'' substantially impairing the model's performance, introducing a major concern for the translation of cutting-edge technology, especially in high-stakes scenarios. We introduce the SegSTRONG-C challenge dedicated to better understanding model deterioration under unforeseen but plausible non-adversarial ``corruption'' and the capabilities of contemporary methods that seek to improve it. Built on a dataset generated through counterfactual robotic replay, SegSTRONG-C provides paired clean and ``corrupted'' samples, enabling reproducible evaluation of model robustness. Participants are challenged to train tool segmentation algorithms on ``uncorrupted'' data and evaluate them on ``corrupted'' test domains for the binary robot tool segmentation task. Through comprehensive baseline experiments and participating submissions from widespread community engagement, SegSTRONG-C reveals key themes for model failure and identifies promising directions for improving robustness. The challenge winners achieved an average of 0.9394 DSC and 0.9301 NSD across the unreleased test sets with ``corruption'' types: bleeding, smoke, and low brightness. This highlights how prior knowledge, customized training strategies, and architectural choice can be leveraged to improve robustness. In conclusion, the SegSTRONG-C challenge has identified practical approaches for enhancing model robustness. However, most approaches rely on conventional techniques that have known limitations. Looking ahead, we advocate for expanding intellectual diversity and creativity in non-adversarial robustness beyond data augmentation.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Dynamic Gaussian Scene Reconstruction by Integrating Events and Structural Priors
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Existing approaches to event-based dynamic Gaussian reconstruction rely on two assumptions for support augmentation and reliability estimation. First, existing Gaussians can absorb reconstruction errors. Second, photometric optimization has converged sufficiently to estimate reliability using analytical variance. Both assumptions can fail under fast motion. When the first fails, regions without Gaussian support cannot generate densification candidates. When the second fails, Gaussians in moving regions where optimization has not converged may be excluded as motion references. We propose Event-Structure Collaborative Dynamic Gaussian Reconstruction (ESC-DGR), using event observations independent of both conditions. Events first identify changes that require additional support, placed only where rendered depth is valid. The augmented representation still needs reliable motion references. Online rendering statistics and historical event evidence therefore propagate displacement estimates from reliable Gaussians to weakly observed neighborhoods. These references describe dominant motion at the frame-interval timescale. Target-time events therefore further condition bounded position residuals for active Gaussians. Support placement, reference selection, and residual prediction thus operate on the same evolving representation within one optimization run. For event-driven monocular dynamic scene reconstruction, our method achieves the best reconstruction quality among the evaluated methods on the E-D3DGS benchmark. Relative to E-D3DGS, dynamic-region PSNR (dPSNR) improves by 1.02 and 1.45 dB on synthetic and real scenes, respectively. The total dynamic Gaussian count across eight synthetic scenes decreases by 8.5%. Although mean frame rate decreases by about 21%-25% relative to E-D3DGS, rendering remains above 80 FPS in all twelve scenes. Code: https://github.com/zh-yu1/ESC-DGR.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: SpectralRoute: Adaptive Spectral Routing for Training-Free Open-Vocabulary Hyperspectral Segmentation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Open-vocabulary semantic segmentation enables the recognition of arbitrary categories through natural language descriptions and has recently been extended from natural images to remote sensing. However, existing approaches primarily focus on three-channel optical imagery or limited-band multispectral data, while pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) struggle to directly exploit the rich spectral information of hyperspectral imagery (HSI) without additional adaptation. More importantly, different land-cover categories rely on distinct spectral cues, which may be weakened by uniform fusion. To address these challenges, we propose SpectralRoute, a training-free framework for open-vocabulary hyperspectral segmentation. Specifically, we construct complementary spectral views from HSI and enrich category descriptions with external spectral knowledge, enabling frozen vision-language models to extract diverse spectral-semantic responses. We then introduce a class-adaptive spectral routing mechanism that selectively amplifies discriminative spectral responses for each category, overcoming the limitations of uniform fusion. Furthermore, physical spectral priors are incorporated to refine predictions for visually similar land-cover categories. Experiments on three hyperspectral benchmarks demonstrate that SpectralRoute consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods without additional training.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Training-Free Continuous Bitrate Control for Scalable Image Coding for Humans and Machines
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Continuous variable-rate compression is highly demanded in real-world applications, but remains underexplored in scalable image coding for humans and machines. In this paper, we propose a training-free variable-rate scalable image coding framework. By adaptively adjusting quantization step sizes based on predicted scale values, the proposed method enables independent and continuous bitrate control for the machine and enhancement layers while preserving important latent information in each layer. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method and highlight the importance of bitrate allocation between the two layers.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Accepted to IEEE 15th Global Conference on Consumer Electronics (IEEE GCCE 2026)

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Generalizable Variable-Rate Adaptation for Image Coding for Machines
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Image Coding for Machines (ICM) aims to preserve task-relevant information for machine vision under limited bitrates. However, most ICM models are trained for a fixed operating point, and extending them to variable-rate compression is challenging because their training objectives differ across tasks and model designs. In this paper, we propose a loss-agnostic distillation framework for variable-rate ICM. A pretrained fixed-rate ICM model is used as a frozen teacher, while a student model learns variable-rate behavior through importance-adaptive quantization and distillation-based optimization. This enables continuous bitrate control with a single model while preserving task-relevant latent components, without requiring the original task-specific loss or downstream task labels. Experiments based on existing ICM models demonstrate that the proposed method provides continuous bitrate control and achieves competitive recognition performance compared with the fixed-rate models.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Accepted to 2026 IEEE International Conference on Visual Communications and Image Processing (IEEE VCIP 2026)

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Bridging the Gap between Continual Learning and Test-Time Adaptation with Domain Preview
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Domain shift is a major problem for training machine learning models. While Continual Learning (CL) assumes distribution shift during training and Continual Test-Time Adaptation (CTTA) considers new domains at test time, setups that require explicit online adaptation to domain shift during both phases remain under-explored. We propose continual learning with domain preview (CL-P), a new combination of CL and TTA where both train and test data suffer from distribution shift. The training phase of CL-P is analogous to domain-incremental learning while the testing phase consists of a TTA phase on a future domain (which we call preview), and an evaluation phase on all seen domains. The model must then adapt to new domains at train and test time. In this paper, we evaluate mainstream CL and TTA methods that adapt only at train or test time, as well as their naive combination. Experimentally, TTA heavily damages the domain on which the CL method has just trained and increases forgetting. Notably, this damage mostly comes from the BatchNorm statistics shared by all domains. In that sense, we propose DOSE (Dosing by Online Statistics of Each domain), which allows a seamless combination of any CL and TTA methods by adaptive domain inference at test time, where the adaptation is applied to each image in proportion to the probability that it comes from the preview domain. Through extensive experiments with ResNet and ViT backbones, various combinations of CL and TTA baseline methods and datasets considering diverse domains, we show that DOSE matches or improves on CL methods alone in all 24 settings and on the naive combination in all but one. The code can be found in appendix.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Motion Mamba 2.0: Autoregressive Diffusion Mamba for Long-Horizon Humanoid Control
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Long-horizon, real-time controllable motion generation is essential for interactive animation and humanoid robotics, where an agent must respond to changing instructions and spatial goals while moving. Existing autoregressive diffusion methods generate motion incrementally, but bounded attention caches limit access to distant history, while repeated denoising introduces substantial inference overhead. We present Motion Mamba 2.0, a Mamba-based root-body diffusion architecture that integrates local attention, resumable recurrent states, and persistent content memory (PCM) for long-horizon controllable motion generation. PCM transforms compressed motion history from Mamba recurrent states, together with state changes and text-conditioned features, into dynamically updated content slots accessible to local attention. To enable efficient inference, we further develop an execution scheme tailored to this architecture, combining CUDA Graph replay, fused kernels, and execution-flow simplification while preserving the canonical history update. Evaluations on retargeted HiPHI demonstrate accurate terminal control over rollouts of up to 39.52 s, while short-horizon comparisons on BONES Seed and retargeted HumanML3D show that the model also retains strong spatial control and text-motion matching. On an RTX 4090, the optimized execution reduces median complete-window latency from 1685.35 to 276.14 ms, achieving a median paired speedup of 6.138$\times$ while preserving identical outputs and committed states in the tested rollouts. Moreover, we conduct extensive real-world evaluation on the Unitree G1, demonstrating sequential text-guided action composition, expressive motion, and interactive locomotion through keyboard and mouse control.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Segment Anything In-Context via Visual Demonstrations
